items.title: I can define homeostasis
items.what: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment despite changes in the external environment. Internal variables are kept within a narrow range, not at a fixed single value.
items.why: This definition is the starting point for explaining why and how regulatory mechanisms exist in all animals.
items.example: Normal human core body temperature is maintained within approximately 36.6–37.5°C even when the external temperature varies from 5°C on a winter morning to 35°C on a summer afternoon.

subtopic.name: Homeostasis Fundamentals
subtopic.what: Introduces the concept of homeostasis and the stimulus-response model that underpins all regulatory mechanisms in living organisms. Covers the key components — stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, and response — and how they work together.
subtopic.why: Understanding homeostasis is foundational to all of VCE Biology Unit 1 AOS2. Without it, the specific regulatory systems (temperature, blood glucose, water) cannot be meaningfully explained or applied.

items.title: I can recall the five stages of a stimulus-response model
items.what: The five stages are: stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, and response. The acronym STRICTER (Stimulus To Receptor, Input to Control, Then Effect and Response) can help recall the sequence.
items.why: Every homeostatic mechanism in the body follows this same pathway, so knowing these five stages allows you to analyse any regulatory process.
items.example: When a phone rings (stimulus), the ears detect it (receptor), the brain decides to answer (control centre), the arm reaches out (effector), and the phone is picked up (response).

items.title: I can describe the stimulus-response model
items.what: A stimulus is a detectable change in the internal or external environment. It is picked up by a receptor, which sends a signal to the control centre. The control centre sends a message to the effector, which produces a response that counteracts the original stimulus.
items.why: Being able to describe the model in full allows you to apply it to biological examples such as temperature, blood glucose, and water balance regulation.
items.example: Placing a hand on a hot stove (stimulus) triggers skin receptors, which send signals to the brain (control centre), which activates arm muscles (effector) to withdraw the hand (response) without conscious thought — a reflex.

items.title: I can explain why homeostasis is important to an organism's survival
items.what: Cells and enzymes function correctly only within narrow ranges of temperature, pH, and chemical concentration. Homeostasis keeps these variables within those ranges, allowing normal metabolism to continue.
items.why: When homeostasis fails, enzyme function deteriorates, cellular processes break down, and the organism may become seriously ill or die.
items.example: Enzymes in the human immune system work more effectively at slightly elevated temperatures during a fever (around 38–39°C), but a sustained temperature above 42°C can cause irreversible brain damage and death.

items.title: I can describe a negative feedback loop using a diagram
items.what: In a negative feedback loop, the response opposes the original stimulus, returning the variable to its set range. The loop is self-limiting: once normal levels are restored, the stimulus disappears and the loop stops.
items.why: Negative feedback is the primary mechanism maintaining homeostasis for temperature, blood glucose, and water balance.
items.example: A household thermostat: if room temperature drops below the set point, the heater turns on. Once the room warms to the set temperature, the thermostat detects this and turns the heater off.

subtopic.name: Feedback Loops
subtopic.what: Covers the two types of feedback loops — negative and positive — including their structures, how they differ, and biological and non-biological examples of each.
subtopic.why: Feedback loops are the core mechanism by which homeostasis is maintained or, in the case of positive feedback, by which certain physiological processes are amplified to completion.

items.title: I can describe a positive feedback loop using a diagram
items.what: In a positive feedback loop, the response amplifies or repeats the original stimulus rather than opposing it. The loop continues until an external event terminates it.
items.why: Positive feedback drives processes that need to be completed rapidly and fully, rather than stabilised, such as childbirth contractions or fruit ripening.
items.example: During childbirth, the baby pressing against the cervix triggers stretch receptors, which cause the brain to signal the pituitary to release oxytocin. Oxytocin causes uterine contractions, which push the baby harder against the cervix, triggering more oxytocin release. This continues until delivery.

subtopic.name: Feedback Loops
subtopic.what: Covers the two types of feedback loops — negative and positive — including their structures, how they differ, and biological and non-biological examples of each.
subtopic.why: Feedback loops are the core mechanism by which homeostasis is maintained or, in the case of positive feedback, by which certain physiological processes are amplified to completion.

items.title: I can distinguish between negative and positive feedback loops
items.what: The key distinction is in the direction of the response relative to the stimulus. Negative feedback opposes the stimulus (self-limiting, maintains stability). Positive feedback reinforces the stimulus (self-amplifying, drives a process to completion).
items.why: Confusing these two types is a common exam error. Being able to distinguish them is explicitly required by the study design.
items.example: Blood glucose regulation is negative feedback: high glucose triggers insulin release, which lowers glucose back to the set range. Oxytocin-driven contractions in labour are positive feedback: contractions cause more oxytocin release, intensifying contractions further until the baby is delivered.

subtopic.name: Feedback Loops
subtopic.what: Covers the two types of feedback loops — negative and positive — including their structures, how they differ, and biological and non-biological examples of each.
subtopic.why: Feedback loops are the core mechanism by which homeostasis is maintained or, in the case of positive feedback, by which certain physiological processes are amplified to completion.

items.title: I can give and explain an example of a positive feedback loop
items.what: A valid example must show that the response increases or reinforces the original stimulus, and that the loop continues until a definitive end point is reached.
items.why: The study design requires students to identify and explain positive feedback, not just negative feedback. Having a clear worked example aids exam responses.
items.example: Ethylene-driven fruit ripening: when the first banana in a bunch ripens, it releases ethylene gas, which causes neighbouring bananas to ripen. Those bananas release more ethylene, accelerating ripening across the bunch — a positive feedback cascade that the fruit industry controls in ripening rooms.

items.title: I can explain how body temperature is detected and where the control centre is located
items.what: Thermoreceptors in the skin detect changes in external temperature. Central thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus and spinal cord detect changes in blood temperature. The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat and coordinates the response.
items.why: Identifying the correct sensor (thermoreceptor) and control centre (hypothalamus) is required for full marks in stimulus-response questions about temperature.
items.example: On a cold morning, skin thermoreceptors detect the drop in external temperature and send signals to the hypothalamus, which then sends signals to blood vessels and muscles to initiate warming responses.

subtopic.name: Temperature Regulation
subtopic.what: Explains how mammals, using humans as the primary example, maintain core body temperature within a narrow range through the hypothalamus, thermoreceptors, and a range of physiological responses including vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating, and shivering.
subtopic.why: Body temperature regulation is a key case study required by the study design and demonstrates how the stimulus-response model and negative feedback apply in a specific physiological context.

items.title: I can describe the physiological responses to an increase in body temperature
items.what: When body temperature rises above the set range, the hypothalamus triggers vasodilation (widening of arterioles near the skin surface, increasing heat loss) and activates sweat glands (sweat evaporates, removing heat). These are cooling responses.
items.why: Understanding these specific effector responses and linking them to heat loss mechanisms is required for exam questions.
items.example: During a run on a 30°C day, arterioles near the skin surface dilate, bringing more warm blood to the surface where heat can radiate away, and sweat glands secrete fluid that evaporates from the skin, each removing heat from the body.

subtopic.name: Temperature Regulation
subtopic.what: Explains how mammals, using humans as the primary example, maintain core body temperature within a narrow range through the hypothalamus, thermoreceptors, and a range of physiological responses including vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating, and shivering.
subtopic.why: Body temperature regulation is a key case study required by the study design and demonstrates how the stimulus-response model and negative feedback apply in a specific physiological context.

items.title: I can describe the physiological responses to a decrease in body temperature
items.what: When body temperature drops below the set range, the hypothalamus triggers vasoconstriction (narrowing of arterioles, reducing heat loss from the skin), shivering (rapid muscle contractions generating heat), and increased secretion of thyroxine and adrenaline to boost metabolic heat production.
items.why: These responses form the basis of exam questions about cold exposure scenarios, such as a hiker spending a night outdoors in near-freezing conditions.
items.example: A hiker in near-freezing temperatures will begin shivering (skeletal muscle contractions produce heat), and arterioles in the skin will constrict so that blood — and its heat — is directed away from the cold skin surface and kept in the body core.

subtopic.name: Temperature Regulation
subtopic.what: Explains how mammals, using humans as the primary example, maintain core body temperature within a narrow range through the hypothalamus, thermoreceptors, and a range of physiological responses including vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating, and shivering.
subtopic.why: Body temperature regulation is a key case study required by the study design and demonstrates how the stimulus-response model and negative feedback apply in a specific physiological context.

items.title: I can explain how vasodilation and vasoconstriction help regulate body temperature
items.what: Blood vessels contain smooth muscle and elastic layers. Vasoconstriction moves blood away from the skin surface, reducing heat loss to the environment. Vasodilation moves blood closer to the skin surface, increasing heat loss.
items.why: The structural basis for vasodilation and vasoconstriction links the stimulus-response model to specific anatomical structures, as required by the study design.
items.example: In the cold, arterioles near the skin surface constrict, so the warm blood is confined to deeper tissues. In the heat, those same arterioles relax and widen, bringing blood close to the surface where heat can dissipate.

subtopic.why: Body temperature regulation is a key case study required by the study design and demonstrates how the stimulus-response model and negative feedback apply in a specific physiological context.

items.title: I can apply the stimulus-response model to temperature regulation using a diagram
items.what: A complete diagram links the stimulus (temperature change), receptor (thermoreceptors), control centre (hypothalamus), effector (blood vessels, sweat glands, muscles), and response (return to 36.6–37.5°C) in a labelled feedback loop.
items.why: Exam questions frequently ask students to construct or annotate diagrams of the temperature regulation feedback loop.
items.example: Stimulus: core temperature rises to 38.5°C. Receptor: hypothalamic thermoreceptors detect the rise. Control centre: hypothalamus signals effectors. Effector: sweat glands activated, arterioles dilate. Response: temperature returns to 37°C.

items.title: I can identify the two hormones involved in blood glucose regulation and their source
items.what: Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. Glucagon is produced by alpha cells in the same structure. The two hormones have opposing effects on blood glucose concentration.
items.why: Correctly identifying the source cells (alpha vs beta) is required for exam responses and is commonly tested.
items.example: After eating a meal, beta cells in the pancreas detect the rise in blood glucose and secrete insulin. During a long exercise session with no food intake, alpha cells detect the fall in blood glucose and secrete glucagon.

subtopic.name: Blood Glucose Regulation
subtopic.what: Explains how insulin and glucagon — produced by beta and alpha cells respectively in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas — maintain blood glucose levels within a normal range through opposing negative feedback loops.
subtopic.why: Blood glucose regulation is a core case study in the study design and provides the physiological context for understanding type 1 diabetes and hypoglycaemia.

items.title: I can explain the role of insulin in blood glucose homeostasis
items.what: When blood glucose rises (e.g. after a meal), beta cells secrete insulin. Insulin promotes glucose uptake by liver, muscle, and fat cells. In liver and muscle, excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage. This lowers blood glucose back to the set range.
items.why: Insulin's mechanism of action is directly tested in short-answer questions and is essential for understanding what goes wrong in type 1 diabetes.
items.example: Two hours after eating a meal containing 80g of carbohydrates, insulin secretion has facilitated glucose uptake by liver and muscle cells, converting the excess to glycogen, and blood glucose has returned to approximately 4–6 mmol/L.

subtopic.name: Blood Glucose Regulation
subtopic.what: Explains how insulin and glucagon — produced by beta and alpha cells respectively in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas — maintain blood glucose levels within a normal range through opposing negative feedback loops.
subtopic.why: Blood glucose regulation is a core case study in the study design and provides the physiological context for understanding type 1 diabetes and hypoglycaemia.

items.title: I can explain the role of glucagon in blood glucose homeostasis
items.what: When blood glucose falls (e.g. during exercise or fasting), alpha cells secrete glucagon. Glucagon stimulates liver cells to break down glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis) and release it into the blood. This raises blood glucose back to the set range.
items.why: Glucagon is the counterpart to insulin and is required to explain the full negative feedback cycle for blood glucose.
items.example: After 6 hours without food, blood glucose has dropped, so alpha cells release glucagon, which signals the liver to break down glycogen stores into glucose, releasing it into the bloodstream to restore the normal range.

subtopic.name: Blood Glucose Regulation
subtopic.what: Explains how insulin and glucagon — produced by beta and alpha cells respectively in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas — maintain blood glucose levels within a normal range through opposing negative feedback loops.
subtopic.why: Blood glucose regulation is a core case study in the study design and provides the physiological context for understanding type 1 diabetes and hypoglycaemia.

items.title: I can apply the stimulus-response model to blood glucose regulation using a diagram
items.what: A complete diagram includes both the high-glucose loop (stimulus: high glucose; receptor: beta cells; effector: liver/muscle/fat cells; response: glucose uptake and glycogen storage) and the low-glucose loop (stimulus: low glucose; receptor: alpha cells; effector: liver cells; response: glycogenolysis).
items.why: The study design requires students to use diagrams and the stimulus-response model to explain blood glucose regulation.
items.example: High blood glucose loop: blood glucose rises after a meal (stimulus) → beta cells detect this (receptor) → insulin secreted (control centre/effector signal) → liver converts glucose to glycogen (effector) → blood glucose falls back to set point (response).

subtopic.name: Blood Glucose Regulation
subtopic.what: Explains how insulin and glucagon — produced by beta and alpha cells respectively in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas — maintain blood glucose levels within a normal range through opposing negative feedback loops.
subtopic.why: Blood glucose regulation is a core case study in the study design and provides the physiological context for understanding type 1 diabetes and hypoglycaemia.

items.title: I can explain what osmoreceptors are and where they are located
items.what: Osmoreceptors are sensors that detect changes in the water concentration (osmotic balance) of the blood. They are located in the hypothalamus. When water concentration falls (e.g. after sweating), osmoreceptors detect this and initiate a response.
items.why: Identifying the receptor type and its location is required for full marks in stimulus-response questions about water balance.
items.example: After a long run during which a person loses 1.5 L of sweat, the water concentration of the blood decreases. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this drop and trigger ADH release.

subtopic.name: Water Balance
subtopic.what: Covers osmoregulation in mammals — how osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in water balance and how ADH acts on the nephron to adjust water reabsorption. Also covers how vascular plants regulate water through stomata and abscisic acid.
subtopic.why: Water balance regulation is the third homeostatic case study required by the study design, and the plant component introduces a different type of regulatory mechanism that is less straightforwardly described as negative feedback.

items.title: I can explain the role of ADH in water balance regulation
items.what: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is released by the pituitary gland in response to signals from the hypothalamus when blood water concentration is low. ADH acts on the collecting duct and distal tubule of the nephron, making them more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed back into the blood and less is excreted in urine.
items.why: ADH is the key effector molecule in mammalian water balance and is directly tested in exam questions about dehydration scenarios.
items.example: During dehydration, ADH increases the water permeability of the collecting duct in the kidney nephron, causing more water to move osmotically from the filtrate back into the surrounding capillaries, producing a small volume of concentrated urine rather than a large volume of dilute urine.

subtopic.name: Water Balance
subtopic.what: Covers osmoregulation in mammals — how osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in water balance and how ADH acts on the nephron to adjust water reabsorption. Also covers how vascular plants regulate water through stomata and abscisic acid.
subtopic.why: Water balance regulation is the third homeostatic case study required by the study design, and the plant component introduces a different type of regulatory mechanism that is less straightforwardly described as negative feedback.

items.title: I can apply the stimulus-response model to water balance in mammals
items.what: The full pathway is: stimulus (decrease in blood water concentration), receptor (osmoreceptors in hypothalamus), control centre (hypothalamus/pituitary), effector (nephron cells in kidney), response (increased water reabsorption, reduced urine output, blood water concentration restored).
items.why: Applying the model to water balance is required by the study design and commonly appears in extended-response exam questions.
items.example: Stimulus: blood water concentration drops after heavy sweating. Receptor: osmoreceptors in hypothalamus detect this. Control centre: hypothalamus signals pituitary. Effector: kidney nephron reabsorbs more water. Response: blood water concentration returns to normal range, urine becomes more concentrated.

subtopic.name: Water Balance
subtopic.what: Covers osmoregulation in mammals — how osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in water balance and how ADH acts on the nephron to adjust water reabsorption. Also covers how vascular plants regulate water through stomata and abscisic acid.
subtopic.why: Water balance regulation is the third homeostatic case study required by the study design, and the plant component introduces a different type of regulatory mechanism that is less straightforwardly described as negative feedback.

items.title: I can explain how water balance is regulated in vascular plants
items.what: When water is scarce, guard cells in plant leaves produce abscisic acid (ABA), which causes potassium ions to be pumped out of the guard cells. Water then leaves the guard cells by osmosis, causing them to become flaccid and the stomata to close, reducing water loss through transpiration.
items.why: Plant water regulation is explicitly listed in the study design and differs meaningfully from animal homeostasis — it is not as clearly a negative feedback mechanism.
items.example: A eucalyptus tree during a dry summer: water stress in leaf cells triggers ABA production, guard cells lose turgor, stomata close, and transpiration stops — but so does gas exchange for photosynthesis, illustrating the trade-off involved.

subtopic.name: Water Balance
subtopic.what: Covers osmoregulation in mammals — how osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in water balance and how ADH acts on the nephron to adjust water reabsorption. Also covers how vascular plants regulate water through stomata and abscisic acid.
subtopic.why: Water balance regulation is the third homeostatic case study required by the study design, and the plant component introduces a different type of regulatory mechanism that is less straightforwardly described as negative feedback.

items.title: I can compare water regulation in plants and animals
items.what: Animals use a clear negative feedback loop with osmoreceptors and ADH to actively regulate water balance. Plants lack an active circulation system and cannot redistribute water internally as readily; stomatal closure reduces water loss but also stops photosynthesis, making plant water regulation a less complete negative feedback mechanism.
items.why: The study design specifically notes that plant water regulation is not straightforwardly described as negative feedback homeostasis, and students are expected to understand why.
items.example: A mammal losing water through sweat triggers ADH, which restores water balance without stopping any other major process. A plant losing water can only close its stomata, which simultaneously halts CO2 uptake and photosynthesis — a significant cost that animals do not face.

subtopic.why: Water balance regulation is the third homeostatic case study required by the study design, and the plant component introduces a different type of regulatory mechanism that is less straightforwardly described as negative feedback.

items.title: I can explain how type 1 diabetes disrupts blood glucose homeostasis
items.what: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the beta cells in the islets of Langerhans. Without beta cells, no insulin is produced. When blood glucose rises, the body cannot lower it, so glucose remains dangerously elevated.
items.why: The study design requires students to explain, using a diagram, how T1D results in a breakdown of blood glucose homeostasis.
items.example: In a glucose tolerance test, a healthy person's blood glucose rises after drinking a glucose solution and then returns to baseline within 2 hours due to insulin. A person with T1D shows a much higher spike that does not return to baseline within the 2-hour window, because no insulin is available to drive glucose uptake.

subtopic.name: Homeostasis Malfunctions
subtopic.what: Examines three conditions arising from failures in homeostatic mechanisms: type 1 diabetes (autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells), hypoglycaemia (blood glucose falling below the normal range), and hyperthyroidism in the form of Graves' disease (autoantibodies driving continuous thyroid hormone production).
subtopic.why: These three conditions are explicitly listed in the study design. Understanding them requires applying feedback loop knowledge to pathological contexts, which is a higher-order skill tested in extended exam questions.

items.title: I can explain the treatment of type 1 diabetes
items.what: Because the body cannot produce insulin, people with T1D must inject synthetic insulin to artificially restore the ability to lower blood glucose. They must also monitor blood glucose levels regularly to determine the correct dose.
items.why: Treatment is explicitly listed in the study design and links back to the mechanism of the condition.
items.example: A person with T1D eats a meal and measures their blood glucose. Based on the reading, they inject an appropriate dose of insulin. The insulin enables liver, muscle, and fat cells to take up glucose, lowering blood glucose back toward the set range — mimicking the normal negative feedback loop.

subtopic.why: These three conditions are explicitly listed in the study design. Understanding them requires applying feedback loop knowledge to pathological contexts, which is a higher-order skill tested in extended exam questions.

items.title: I can define hypoglycaemia and explain how it differs from type 1 diabetes
items.what: Hypoglycaemia is a condition in which blood glucose falls below the normal homeostatic range. It is the opposite of the elevated blood glucose seen in T1D. Common causes include insufficient food intake, excessive exercise, or (in people with T1D) too much insulin.
items.why: The study design requires students to define hypoglycaemia and distinguish it from T1D. Confusing the direction of the glucose dysregulation is a common error.
items.example: A marathon runner who has not eaten for several hours may develop hypoglycaemia (blood glucose too low) and become dizzy or confused. Consuming a glucose gel restores blood glucose. By contrast, untreated T1D results in blood glucose that is too high, not too low.

subtopic.why: These three conditions are explicitly listed in the study design. Understanding them requires applying feedback loop knowledge to pathological contexts, which is a higher-order skill tested in extended exam questions.

items.title: I can explain how the normal thyroid hormone feedback loop works
items.what: The hypothalamus releases thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). TSH stimulates the thyroid gland to produce T3 and T4. High levels of T3 and T4 inhibit both the hypothalamus and pituitary (negative feedback), reducing TRH and TSH and thus slowing T3/T4 production.
items.why: Understanding the normal loop is a prerequisite for explaining how Graves' disease disrupts it. This three-gland axis (hypothalamus–pituitary–thyroid) is a commonly examined structure.
items.example: When T3 and T4 levels are adequate, they feed back to the hypothalamus and pituitary, suppressing TRH and TSH. With less TSH stimulation, the thyroid produces less T3/T4, and levels gradually fall, at which point the inhibition lifts and the cycle restarts.

subtopic.what: Examines three conditions arising from failures in homeostatic mechanisms: type 1 diabetes (autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing beta cells), hypoglycaemia (blood glucose falling below the normal range), and hyperthyroidism in the form of Graves' disease (autoantibodies driving continuous thyroid hormone production).
subtopic.why: These three conditions are explicitly listed in the study design. Understanding them requires applying feedback loop knowledge to pathological contexts, which is a higher-order skill tested in extended exam questions.

items.title: I can explain how Graves' disease disrupts thyroid hormone homeostasis
items.what: In Graves' disease, the immune system produces autoantibodies that bind to and continuously stimulate TSH receptors on the thyroid gland. This forces the thyroid to keep producing T3 and T4 regardless of the feedback inhibition from the hypothalamus and pituitary. The negative feedback loop cannot function because the stimulus (autoantibody binding) is not regulated by hormone levels.
items.why: The study design requires students to explain, using a diagram, how hyperthyroidism in the form of Graves' disease occurs.
items.example: Normally, high T3/T4 would suppress TRH and TSH, reducing thyroid stimulation. In Graves' disease, autoantibodies continue to activate the TSH receptor directly, so T3/T4 levels remain elevated regardless of how much TRH and TSH are suppressed. The result is continuous overproduction of thyroid hormones, causing symptoms such as bulging eyes, anxiety, weight loss, and irregular heartbeat.
